articles.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.content: Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority , adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.” That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content. Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health. This is what the policy says: “You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.” “Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.” If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.
articles.summary: 谷歌更新隐私政策，为个性化AI功能新增例外条款，可能用Gmail、Drive和Google Photos数据投放定向广告。

articles.title: UUIDv7 doesn't have the properties you think it does
articles.content: Built on Shards of Silicon This post is part of a collection on UUIDs . I’m going to call it. UUIDv7 is weird. Most blog posts about UUIDv7 tout these benefits: monotonically increasing IDs a helpful timestamp of when the object was created; and unguessable IDs But none of these properties are strictly held. Certain RFC compliant implementations of UUIDv7 violate these properties to extreme degrees. The only useful property UUIDv7 appears to strictly provide is uniqueness and therefore collision resistance. I’ve already discussed how UUIDv7 IDs can be guessable , so this post explores the other properties. Is the timestamp useful? Superficially, it seems that embedding a timestamp in the ID can remove the need to track the creation time in a separate database column, providing marginally more efficient database operations. If you need to list things ordered by creation time very often, it’s useful if the primary index gives that behavior, removing the need for another index. Unfortunately, the timestamp embedded in a UUIDv7 ID may not relate to the object creation time. The Postgres docs for uuid_extract_timestamp helpfully warn that “the extracted timestamp is not necessarily exactly equal to the time the UUID was generated”. RFC 9562 allows implementations to alter the timestamp field, using values that aren’t strictly derived from the system clock. This relates to the tension between UUID monotonicity and timestamp accuracy. In certain scenarios, the difference between the timestamp and the current time can be arbitrarily large. Implementations MAY alter the actual timestamp. — RFC 9562 §6.1 This specification makes no requirement or guarantee about how close the clock value needs to be to the actual time. — RFC 9562 §6.1 … implementations MAY increment the timestamp ahead of the actual time … — RFC 9562 §6.2 Incrementing the timestamp ahead of the system clock is an interesting problem. If the generator is seeing so much load that a counter field is regularly overflowing then the timestamp could accelerate into the future. Using a sufficiently large counter would be wise and the RFC says the minimum size SHOULD be 12 bits. A counter overflow would require a pretty aggressive creation rate, over 4,096 IDs per millisecond per node, which is beyond the limits of many systems. This overflow becomes relevant, however, if the timestamp freezes; which I’ll discuss in a later section. Example: Python uuid.uuid7() One prominent implementation that increments the timestamp is the Python standard library’s UUIDv7. The increment happens only in certain circumstances, like when the counter overflows. Unfortunately, the generator can get stuck in an increment cycle if the clock ever jumps backwards and the timestamp can race ahead of the system time by an arbitrarily large amount. Here’s a simple example: import uuid from datetime import datetime # Prime the generator with the current time t = uuid.uuid7().time now = datetime.now() delta = (datetime.fromti

articles.title: The Real Kevin Bacon
articles.content: Robert De Niro : one movie away from Kevin Bacon. Cillian Murphy : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. Ryan Gosling : one movie away from Kevin Bacon. Tom Hanks : one movie away from Kevin Bacon. Benedict Cumberbatch : one movie away from Kevin Bacon. Meryl Streep : one movie away from Kevin Bacon. Timothée Chalamet : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. Saoirse Ronan : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. Anya Taylor-Joy : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. Jessie Buckley : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. Austin Butler : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. Margot Robbie : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. Emma Stone : one movie away from Kevin Bacon. Zendaya : two movies away from Kevin Bacon. The “Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon” is a game where players try to connect any actor to Kevin Bacon in fewer than six steps, where each step links two actors who co-starred in a film. The conventional wisdom is that Kevin Bacon is the all-encompassing center of Hollywood, so prolific that the game is a lot easier than if it were called the “Six Degrees of John Doe.” For example, Kevin Bacon’s remoteness is 2.28: so an actor is, on average, 2.28 degrees from Kevin Bacon. But 2.28 degrees is not the best remoteness score. Kevin Bacon ranks 175th among all Hollywood actors. Can you guess who’s #1? Philip Seymour Hoffman ranks #250. Keep going… Samuel L. Jackson is the center of Hollywood , with a remoteness of just 2.09. Willem Dafoe is second at 2.13, and Robert De Niro follows at 2.14. Women are underrepresented among the top 100, taking only 16 spots. Nicole Kidman is the highest-ranking woman at #21. Let’s create a time machine for the center of Hollywood and calculate actors’ remoteness in previous years. Our time machine starts at the end of 2025. Go back in time Let’s time travel to 2006, when Samuel L. Jackson took the crown. Kevin Bacon still does not appear; his highest rank was #108 in 1996 after his role in “Sleepers.” We can view all centers of Hollywood since 1980. Use the slider to look around. How might we predict who will take the crown from Samuel L. Jackson? Let’s apply this idea to the future . To do that, we need to find what affects an actor’s remoteness score. One obvious metric is film count. Indeed, Samuel L. Jackson appeared in far more films than anyone else in our 169,000 actor dataset. Nicolas Cage, who’s the next closest, appeared in 96 films. While the relationship between film count and remoteness is strong, it doesn't fully explain actors’ scores. For example, Natalie Portman and Anna Kendrick differ significantly in their remoteness, despite appearing in the same number of films. The difference between Natalie Portman and Anna Kendrick lies in their co-stars: Natalie Portman is cast in films with more prolific actors than Anna Kendrick. Of the 250 most-connected actors, Natalie Portman has worked with almost three times as many as Anna Kendrick has. articles.title: Canadians are running out of time to oppose Bill C-22
articles.content: Canada’s Parliament is debating a massive expansion of surveillance powers that will threaten the privacy and security of millions of people. Bill C-22, also called the Lawful Access Act, has already passed the House of Commons, and is now before the Canadian Senate. Canadians still have an opportunity to speak out and stop this dangerous legislation. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA) is urging all Canadians to sign its petition opposing the bill. (The petition on CCLA’s website is governed by CCLA’s privacy policy.) Take action Tell the canadian senate to stop C-22 As we wrote earlier this year , Bill C-22 gives the government new powers to force digital services—including telecom companies, messaging apps, and more—to help with government surveillance. Worse, it allows Canada’s Minister of Public Safety to order companies to create a backdoor to their services for law enforcement, as long as it doesn’t lead to a “systemic insecurity.” That’s a clear recipe for weakening the encryption we all rely on. It also requires services to retain metadata for up to a year, which reveals who people communicate with, where they go, and what services they use, even when they are not suspected of any crime. Researchers at CCLA and Citizen Lab published a detailed analysis of C-22 and its serious constitutional and cybersecurity problems. The analysis points out that the bill needs more than cosmetic changes—it calls for entirely withdrawing Part 2 of Bill C-22, the section that establishes the surveillance and data retention regime. Bill C-22 could also expand the sharing of Canadians’ personal data with foreign law enforcement, including the United States. Canada has been negotiating a cross-border data-sharing agreement with the U.S. that would allow American police to get information about Canadian internet users without any Canadian court oversight. Some Canadian senators have already expressed concerns about the bill, and rightly suggested, as CCLA and Citizen Lab have, that it may not be compatible with privacy protections in the Canadian constitution. If you’re in Canada, read and sign CCLA’s petition opposing Bill C-22 today. Don’t let the Senate allow this dangerous expansion of government surveillance to become Canada’s new reality. Take action Canadians: defend your privacy and security

articles.title: WorldTUI: I trained a 360M model to pretend to be a terminal
articles.content: TL;DR: I fine-tuned a 360M-parameter language model to act as a terminal. There's no shell or filesystem behind it: every keypress goes in, and the model predicts how the screen changes. It can create files, run vim and tmux, play snake, and usually remembers what you wrote a few commands later. The biggest wins were teaching it to repair its own mistakes and decoding screen rows in parallel. Try it in your browser (208 MB) and type pythoon to see that it's not a real shell. The demo is designed for a desktop browser with WebGPU and a physical keyboard. Chrome or Edge is the best place to try it. It should work on a modern phone, but painfully slowly. When I first saw Genie 3 last year, I started imagining a future where applications aren't written in code but learned. Instead of a game engine rendering the scene, a model predicts the next most likely frame from the user's inputs. Naturally I wanted to train my own world model. But I don't have a massive GPU cluster or a pile of video data, so I scaled down my ambition: instead of a game world, a terminal. A terminal turned out to be a good fit. It's just a grid of characters rather than pixels, and I can generate as much perfectly labelled training data as I want by running real shells. A pretrained language model also already has a pretty good idea of what ls or cat should print. What I really wanted to know was whether it could maintain a consistent world, or just generate convincing terminal output. The final model is based on Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B, fine-tuned on terminal sessions recorded from real programs running inside Docker. Jump to example videos How it sees a terminal Standard LLMs take a prompt and then append tokens to the end, one at a time. That doesn't map well to a terminal. A single keypress can do something on its own, like esc in vim, and output doesn't always go to the bottom: clear wipes the screen and sends the cursor back to the top. So instead of predicting a stream of text, I need to predict changes to the screen. I treat the terminal as a grid of characters, one per cell. The model doesn't see the grid directly, but a sequence of tokens describing its contents and the changes made to it. A session Every session starts with a snapshot: the screen size, its contents and where the cursor is. The size is part of the input, not fixed at 32×96. In the demo, you can set the rows and columns when creating a custom starting screen. BOS SCREEN_START 32 96 ROW_0 0 'simedw@laptop:~$ ' CURSOR 0 17 1 SCREEN_END This also lets me start partway through an application. Give it a bash prompt, vim buffer or a game of snake, and the model tries to continue from there. (It does better from bash.) After that, each keypress goes in as the raw bytes a real terminal would send. Letters are themselves, Enter is \r , Escape is 0x1b and ← is ESC [ D and so on. INPUT_START 'l' INPUT_END The model answers with which rows to rewrite and where the cursor ends up: OUTPUT_START ROW_0 17 'l' CURSOR 0 18 1

articles.title: The glorious @xkcdRandom Zig builtin
articles.content: One of my favorite xkcd comics of all time is Random Number . The image depicts a C function that supposedly returns a random integer, but in reality always returns 4 . I was reminded of this wonderful comic a few days ago, due to a security incident where people accidentally used the number 4 (among others) instead of a properly generated sequence of random bytes. Satire has a tendency to become reality, I guess. Since there is a clear demand among developers for the xkcd random number generator, I’m of the opinion that self-respecting languages should ship a built-in implementation. I’m here today to lead by example, as I unveil the glorious @xkcdRandom builtin for the Zig language. Can you guess what it does? Indeed, it returns the number 4 ! Now go found a multi-billion-dollar startup on top of this genius idea. But why? Why not? After completing the Ziglings exercises and brain-coding a toy minesweeper game , I felt like my grasp of the language was solid enough to attempt something more ambitious. I wanted to get my hands on production-grade Zig code, and play with it to see how the different pieces of the language fit together. Hacking on the Zig compiler sounded like the perfect idea! Builtins vs. functions A sane person might implement the xkcd RNG as a literal port of the original C code, which maps to the following Zig function: fn xkcdRandom () i32 { return 4 ; // chosen by fair dice roll. // guaranteed to be random. } There’s one very big drawback to this approach: it’s boring. Don’t get me wrong, I like boring and low-maintenance code as much as the next person… but this time my goal is to learn , not to produce . I actually want to jump through hoops and make things overly complicated! Builtins are perfect for this. They are, as the name suggests, built-in constructs in the Zig language. Adding one means I get to fork and modify the compiler. Yay! Builtin implementation and usage The builtin source code is intertwined with the rest of the Zig compiler, so it’s not really possible to include it here. Feel free to inspect the diff if you are curious (it’s just 22 lines), or to clone my Zig fork and check out the 0.17.x-xkcd branch. With these changes to the compiler, you can build programs like the one below. Isn’t that neat? const std = @import( "std" ); pub fn main (_: std.process.Init) ! void { const someRandomNumber: usize = @xkcdRandom(); const anotherRandomNumber: f32 = @xkcdRandom(); std.debug. print ( "The random numbers you ordered just arrived: {}, {} \n " , .{ someRandomNumber, anotherRandomNumber } ); } Hacking on Zig is surprisingly straightforward The Zig developers have clearly put effort into developer experience. You can build Zig with a single command: zig build --zig-lib=lib -Dno-lib -Ddev=x86_64-linux . The fresh build took roughly a minute to complete on my laptop, which in my book is quite good for a compiler. Subsequent builds were faster. As for the coding work itself, an LLM pointed me to the file where built

articles.title: Software is slow because of bad design, not slow languages
articles.content: Many people are saying that AI will make software faster by rewriting it in faster languages, but this isn’t generally true. Most programs cannot be meaningfully sped up by rewriting them in C or Rust. How can this be true? Some languages are orders-of-magnitude faster than others: for instance, C can be fifty times faster than Python. Won’t rewriting my Python program in C thus make it fifty times faster? No, it won’t. Software performance is usually dominated by I/O, not the speed of the language. Where language speed matters, most slow languages already have popular libraries that allow them to unlock C-like speed. In general, performance is a matter of design , not of language choice. Most real programs are I/O-bound Consider a simple CRUD website with a database. For any given request, 50% of the request time might be spent querying the database: to fetch the current user, the record being asked for, any relevant user memberships or settings, and so on. Rewriting that website in C can only speed up that other 50%, which puts a hard ceiling on the improvements you can make . At best, you’ll make requests twice as fast (probably closer to 1.5x in practice). That’s not bad, but it’s nowhere near an order-of-magnitude speedup. In other words, most real programs are “I/O-bound”: they spend most of their time waiting for data to be input or output somewhere, as opposed to “CPU-bound” programs that spend most of their time actively doing things. I/O-bound programs don’t just have to rely on a database. Often programs have to wait on some third-party API, or on writing or reading data to disk. You could speed the code in curl up by 100x and you probably wouldn’t even notice, because curl spends all of its time waiting on the network. Slow languages already delegate work to fast languages What about work that is obviously not I/O-bound? For instance, wikis have to turn stored markdown into renderable HTML . Wouldn’t rewriting that in a faster language cause a massive speedup? It would! That’s why applications that do that use libraries like cmark-gfm that call out to fast languages for markdown rendering. In general, most slow languages can write very fast programs by invoking this kind of library. Python is famously a slow language, but it’s a competitive choice for CPU-bound workloads like machine learning and mathematics, because it has a healthy set of libraries that let it offload these workloads to fast C code. If a Python program spends 80% of its time doing matrix multiplications on a GPU, you are very unlikely to be able to speed it up by rewriting it in C, because those matrix multiplications are already happening in tightly-optimized C or assembly code. Of course, some programs do in fact do a lot of CPU-bound work in slow languages. If a program has not had much engineering attention, there will probably be a lot of low-hanging fruit . But these programs are often unimportant: if they were important, someone would have gone in and optimiz

articles.title: How close can pure FP get to C?
articles.content: How close can pure FP get to C? October 22, 2026 In Why Lean is Faster Than Rust , the author shares an impressive result: a DEFLATE compression library written in Lean 4 , a functional programming language and proof assistant, outperforming an equivalent Rust package that crates.io says has been downloaded over a billion times. From the article: lean-zip beats every single compression level miniz_oxide provides, i.e. we're capable of providing the same compression at higher throughput. At its fastest setting we're 15% quicker and the output is 8.8% smaller. However, the article also notes that while they managed to surpass Rust's miniz_oxide , they were no match for the end boss of DEFLATE performance: libdeflate , written in C. lean-zip is certainly not the best here: libdeflate unsurprisingly blows it out of the water (unsurprisingly because this is a very carefully tuned implementation using architecture-specific SIMD, that we can't touch in Lean). Enter Roc , a functional programming language (but not a theorem prover) with an explicit focus on runtime performance. Roc's tagline is "Fast, Friendly, Functional," and Fast comes first because both running fast and compiling fast have always been central goals. Roc is not a mature language (it's still weeks away from its first numbered release, 0.1.0), and its nascent package ecosystem has had almost no optimization work done on it. Still, between its language design, longstanding optimizations , and brand-new compiler implementation , I figured Roc already had enough of a foundation in place to take on the champ: libdeflate. So I spent a bunch of time grinding through performance optimizations on roc-deflate , a package Niclas Ahden wrote (and uses in paid production work ) for DEFLATE compression. I didn't expect to beat libdeflate's performance across the board, but I wanted to see how close it could get on the non-streaming APIs (as roc-deflate hasn't implemented streaming yet), using the classic Silesia corpus for benchmarking and verifying that it produced identical outputs. Here's where the benchmarks stand today, running on the 2021 M1 MacBook Pro where I did all the optimization work, as well as on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X Ubuntu machine for an x64 comparison. roc-deflate ran these 144 benchmarks slower on average than libdeflate, in the median case 8.9% slower on the Ryzen 3900X, and 2.6% on the M1 MacBook Pro. M1 MacBook Pro Ryzen 3900X Ubuntu MB/s 700 600 500 400 300 200 100 0 Compression Level MB/s 700 600 500 400 300 200 100 0 file that ran fastest file that ran slowest L1 libdeflate roc-deflate Compression Level So while we didn't outperform the champ on average, a median slowdown percentage in the single digits compared to such a carefully-tuned SIMD-powered C library is wild. It's frankly not a result I knew was achievable going in, since Roc is a functional language with automatic memory management racing against code that doesn't have to do bounds checks. articles.title: Docker is weird
articles.content: I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird . Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker. Containers aren’t real Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc. Containers really aren’t real There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat. Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network. Images are just folders Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root ) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash , Docker is going to: Download the ubuntu image from Dockerhub. Put that image somewhere. Run /some/weird/docker/path/bin/bash Go is kind of a terrible language for a container runtime Docker’s container runtime, runc , is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Go’s runtime is natively multi-threaded. That’s a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc . Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Go’s runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls. Go also doesn’t have fork! Fork only forks the main thread, so it’s kind of a footgun in a runtime like Go’s. But a container runtime really wants to fork, set up a bunch of restrictions, and then exec the process you actually put in docker run . To get around this, runc execs /proc/self/exe with a special command line arguement that identifies it as a child process to approximate a fork. Docker requires root! This is pretty easy to miss if you, like me, run Docker in MacOS. Many of the Linux kernel APIs that container runtimes use require, or at least used to, to be run as root, so the Docker daemon usually runs as root. I can only imagine that container security is a very tough job. This seems better these days. The big exception seems to be networking. If you’re running a rootless container runtime, it looks like it has to reimplement the whole networking stack in userspace to actually give you the same features! Learning is fun! I’ve only just started my own container runtime, and I already feel like I’ve learned so much about Docker. Writing your own version of a tool you use is a great way to learn about it!
articles.summary: 作者自制容器运行时后总结Docker的怪异之处，指出容器本质只是受特殊限制的进程，并非虚拟机。

articles.title: Please don't mess with links
articles.content: Please don't mess with links: 2026-05-31 A link is just a button that takes you somewhere when you click it right? < style > span { text-decoration : underline ; color : #44EEEE ; } </ style > < span onclick = "window.location='https://xkcd.com/'" >100% legit link</ span > 100% legit link Except that's a pale, shallow imitation of a link. A real link can be: Opened in a new tab. (ctrl) ... or a fresh window. (shift) ... or saved as a file (alt). Copied as a URL (right click) Used with the keyboard (tab + enter) Seen by tools like search engines and screen readers. Hovered over to see the URL. ... none of which work with a button. Another common offense is to use a real link, but hook the click event to open a popup. However, with a real <a target="_blank"> link, I can: See the loading progress... ... or/and cancel it. ... see descriptive error pages and retry if needed. Open multiple at once. Read the original page while it loads. Use my browser's tabs or/and window manager to organize them. Bookmark the page. Copy the URL and send it to a friend. ... and above all, they are consistent: I've long lost count of how many times I've accidentally closed the whole site while trying to close a popup that was a little too convincing. It's also extremely common to click a link with a slow connection, only to be greeted with perpetual spinner. I have no idea if anything is actually happening or how long it will take. Worse, it usually covers up the original page so I can't even read that! Browsers are good at links and loading pages: It's the whole point. Don't use javascript buttons as links. Don't build your own loading animations. Link previews should open and close on hover, not on click. Don't open links in javascript popups: Use target="_blank" instead. Other common problems : Infinite scrolling breaks ctrl-f, bookmarks, the home/end keys and often the back button. You can have a 100k of text on a page: Browsers will render partially downloaded HTML and the user won't even notice. Using a 5 MB javascript framework just do a worse job of downloading text is dumb. To optimize speed, it's best to minimize the total number of round trips. Just putting everything in a single TCP connection will always be better than breaking it up because of TCP's slow start algorithm. Don't reimplement <details> which will break search tools and screen readers. ... but using fancy CSS to make it look nice is fine. Don't roll your own date picker (or any other built-in form inputs) This will always used the user's preferred date format, covert it to the standard yyyy-mm-dd, and works with the keyboard... also, it's one line of code that works with dark mode by default. Related : Real links!

articles.title: Debunking "Faster than Rust": Malicious Benchmarks in Tov
articles.content: Tov is a new programming language marketed to be "[a] programming language for coding agents. It reads like TypeScript and builds native binaries that beat Rust's." Benchmarks in their Git repository show that they perform better than Rust, in some cases over 10× better. However, they also briefly mentioned the internals of Tov: Tov is a compiler. It checks the TypeScript your agent wrote, writes it out as C and hands that to clang, so what you ship is one native binary with nothing to install next to it. A sane engineer would immediately doubt the correctness of their benchmarks. Rust has pretty much the same performance as C, and if Tov transpiles to C, saying Tov beats Rust is mostly equivalent to saying C beats C . That's contradiction right there. Let's ignore the stats for axum , maybe tokio has some overhead, like maybe ; but clearly there's no way you get 1.6× faster than Rust in strings . You have to be lying. That's what a sane engineer would normally think. In this blog post, we check 3 of their "inflated" benchmarks: bigint_fib , dispatch , and map_insert . We show that these benchmarks are maliciously crafted to slow Rust down . We have also benchmarked the improved Rust programs with their Tov programs to show that Rust has equivalent or better performance than Tov . Set-ups cargo build --release was used to compile the Rust programs, and tov build (which defaults to -O3 ) was used to compile the Tov programs. articles.title: a hacky fucked up way to portably access errno from outside of c
articles.content: here's something really cursed i made a while back. the goal here is to create a portable way to obtain the value of errno from outside of c, without using a wrapper function written in c. for those unaware, errno is defined as a macro, and its expansion is non-portable and usually comes with no stability guarantees. so if you're calling libc functions from some other language (such as hare, which i'll be using in this post), it's not possible to retrieve error values from them without relying on an implementation detail or writing a wrapper function in c which returns errno. ...unless you're willing to resort to some fucked up hacks, that is. preamble use io; use sys; use types::c; @symbol("close") fn c_close(fd: int) int; @symbol("dup") fn c_dup(oldfd: int) int; @symbol("dup2") fn c_dup2(oldfd: int, newfd: int) int; @symbol("lseek") fn c_lseek(fd: int, offs: io::off, whence: int) io::off; @symbol("mkstemp") fn c_mkstemp(template: *c::char) int; @symbol("perror") fn c_perror(s: nullable *c::char) void; @symbol("read") fn c_read(fd: int, buf: *opaque, count: size) c::ssize; @symbol("strerror") fn c_strerror(errnum: int) *c::char; @symbol("unlink") fn c_unlink(path: *c::char) int; @symbol("write") fn c_write(fd: int, buf: *opaque, count: size) c::ssize; def SEEK_SET = 0; def STDERR_FILENO = 2i; there aren't any libc functions which return the value of errno. there are, however, functions which return a string that describes errno. so let's start there. export type error = !str; standard c defines two promising functions: strerror and perror. posix defines two more functions: strerror_r and strerror_l . unfortunately, the strerror functions all take in the error number as an argument. only perror reads from errno directly. perror prints an error string to stderr, so our goal now to is to somehow capture the error string from perror , without actually writing anything to stderr. alright, so let's do it. during program initialization, i dup STDERR_FILENO (2), open a temporary file, and change STDERR_FILENO to refer to the temporary file: let stderr = -1; let tmpfd = -1; let tmpname: [_]u8 = ['/', 't', 'm', 'p', '/', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', 'X', '\0']; @init fn stderr_tmp() void = { stderr = c_dup(STDERR_FILENO); assert(stderr != -1); tmpfd = c_mkstemp(&tmpname: *c::char); assert(tmpfd != -1); const n = c_dup2(tmpfd, STDERR_FILENO); assert(n != -1); }; @fini fn stderr_tmp() void = { if (tmpfd != -1) { c_close(tmpfd); c_unlink(&tmpname: *c::char); }; }; all low-level functions (libc wrappers or syscall wrappers) which may interact with stderr will silently adjust the fd from STDERR_FILENO to the dup'd stderr file descriptor if necessary. (i'll give an example later on, if you're confused by that.) when an error occurs, the below function is called to obtain the error string: fn get_errno() error = { c_perror(null); if (c_write(STDERR_FILENO, &0u8, 1) == -1) { return "Unknown error"; }; c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO, 0, SEEK_SET); defer c_lseek(STDERR_FILENO,

articles.title: a neat trick i found for reusing physical memory
articles.content: i found a neat trick which lets you take advantage of CoW to duplicate memory without allocating anything upfront. maybe some people already know about this, but i just discovered it and i think it's cool (and i kinda wish it was easier to take advantage of this with higher-level stdlib functions) start by creating a memory-backed file descriptor and mmaping it (error handling omitted): int fd = memfd_create("foo", MFD_CLOEXEC); ftruncate(fd, SIZE); char *template = mmap(NULL, SIZE, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0); write some "template" to it (this is what will be dup'd later): memset(template, 67, SIZE); now, to allocate a chunk of memory with this template, use mmap with MAP_PRIVATE : char *copy = mmap(NULL, SIZE, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0); this is cool because regardless of the size of the initial allocation, the copy isn't taking up any physical memory. and say you mutate the copy now: copy[i] = 69; this will only allocate a single page of memory (4 KiB); the rest of the pages are still shared with the original template! i did a test here where i allocated 32 MiB, and then "copied" it with what would be another 32 MiB allocation, but the total physical memory usage was 32.004 MiB. i wonder if it would be possible to do this with a continuous memory region. like, 32 MiB of virtual memory, but because it's all filled with the same (non-zero) stuff, only 1 page of physical memory is allocated upfront. this feels like it could be useful maybe

articles.title: php/php-src (C)
articles.content: PHP is a popular general-purpose scripting language that is especially suited to web development. Fast, flexible and pragmatic, PHP powers everything from your blog to the most popular websites in the world. PHP is distributed under the Modified BSD License (SPDX-License-Identifier: BSD-3-Clause ). The PHP manual is available at php.net/docs . Prebuilt packages and binaries Prebuilt packages and binaries can be used to get up and running fast with PHP. For Windows, the PHP binaries can be obtained from windows.php.net . After extracting the archive the *.exe files are ready to use. For other systems, see the installation chapter . For Windows, see Build your own PHP on Windows . For a minimal PHP build from Git, you will need autoconf, bison, and re2c. For a default build, you will additionally need libxml2 and libsqlite3. On Ubuntu, you can install these using: sudo apt install -y pkg-config build-essential autoconf bison re2c libxml2-dev libsqlite3-dev On Fedora, you can install these using: sudo dnf install re2c bison autoconf make ccache libxml2-devel sqlite-devel On MacOS, you can install these using brew : brew install autoconf bison re2c libiconv libxml2 sqlite or with MacPorts : sudo port install autoconf bison re2c libiconv libxml2 sqlite3 Generate configure: Configure your build. --enable-debug is recommended for development, see ./configure --help for a full list of options. # For development ./configure --enable-debug # For production ./configure Build PHP. To speed up the build, specify the maximum number of jobs using the -j argument: The number of jobs should usually match the number of available cores, which can be determined using nproc . PHP ships with an extensive test suite, the command make test is used after successful compilation of the sources to run this test suite. Tests run in parallel by default, using up to 10 detected logical processors. Set -jN in TEST_PHP_ARGS or TESTS to override the worker count: make TEST_PHP_ARGS=-j4 test This runs make test with a maximum of 4 concurrent jobs. Alternatively, use -j1 to run tests sequentially. Use the TEST_PHP_ARGS or TESTS variable to test only specific directories: make TESTS=tests/lang/ test The qa.php.net site provides more detailed info about testing and quality assurance. Installing PHP built from source After a successful build (and test), PHP may be installed with: Depending on your permissions and prefix, make install may need superuser permissions. Extensions provide additional functionality on top of PHP. PHP consists of many essential bundled extensions. Additional extensions can be found on the PIE Extensions list, and installed with 🥧 PIE, the PHP Installer for Extensions or the deprecated PHP Extension Community Library - PECL . The PHP source code is located in the Git repository at github.com/php/php-src . Contributions are most welcome by forking the repository and sending a pull request. Discussions are done on GitHub, but depending on the topic can also be r

articles.title: nodejs/node (JavaScript)
articles.content: Node.js is an open-source, cross-platform JavaScript runtime environment. For information on using Node.js, see the Node.js website . The Node.js project uses an open governance model . The OpenJS Foundation provides support for the project. Contributors are expected to act in a collaborative manner to move the project forward. We encourage the constructive exchange of contrary opinions and compromise. The TSC reserves the right to limit or block contributors who repeatedly act in ways that discourage, exhaust, or otherwise negatively affect other participants. This project has a Code of Conduct . Looking for help? Check out the instructions for getting support . Node.js follows semantic versioning . Alpha : Under active development where semver-major changes are allowed. Each October, a new release line (for example, Node.js 27) branches off main and receives Alpha releases (for example, 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 ) for 6 months, then are promoted to Current (see below) each April. Alpha releases are signed, tagged, and tested through CITGM , but their API and ABI may change between releases. They are intended for library authors and CI pipelines, not for production use. Current : Under active development, no semver-major changes allowed. Node.js releases a new major version once a year, in April. Releases stay Current for 6 months, then convert to LTS (see below) each October. Their ABI may change between releases. They are intended for library authors and CI pipelines, not for production use. LTS : Releases under Long Term Support, with a focus on stability and security. Only changes that have been on Alpha or Current release for two weeks can be backported to a typical LTS release. Every major version becomes an LTS release, and receives 30 months of LTS support, for a total of 36 months from its first Current release to End-of-Life. LTS release lines have alphabetically-ordered code names, beginning with Node.js 4 Argon. Nightly : Code from the main branch built every 24-hours when there are changes. Unlike Alpha releases, nightly builds are automated and untested. Use with caution. Release lines up to and including Node.js 26 follow the previous schedule, where a new major version was released every 6 months and only even-numbered major versions became LTS. See the Node.js release schedule announcement for details. For more information, see the Release README . Binaries, installers, and source tarballs are available at https://nodejs.org/en/download/ . https://nodejs.org/download/release/ The latest directory is an alias for the latest Current release. The latest- codename directory is an alias for the latest release from an LTS line. For example, the latest-hydrogen directory contains the latest Hydrogen (Node.js 18) release. https://nodejs.org/download/nightly/ Each directory and filename includes the version (e.g., v22.0.0 ), followed by the UTC date (e.g., 20240424 for April 24, 2024), and the short commit SHA of the HEAD of the release (e.g.,

articles.title: Three things you should know about permafrost
articles.content: How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it. The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two…

articles.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
articles.content: Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs. What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs…
articles.summary: MIT科技评论指出AI推理成本被忽视的一面：模型响应后产生的大量后端数据带来隐性存储开销。

articles.title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
articles.content: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. articles.title: We can do impossible things
articles.content: I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.” I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker:…

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 Review: The Littlest Smartphone That Could
articles.content: Samsung’s cute compact is for those who want the smallest possible phone. Performance and camera are solid, but it’s pricier than its predecessor.
articles.summary: WIRED评测三星Galaxy Z Flip8：主打最小巧机身，性能与相机表现扎实，但价格高于前代。

articles.title: Split Tunneling Is Your VPN’s Best Feature. Here’s How to Make the Most of It
articles.content: This feature common to VPN services gives you protection and privacy specifically when and where you need it.
articles.summary: WIRED介绍VPN分流隧道功能，可按需在特定场景启用保护与隐私，并给出实用配置建议。

articles.title: Turtle Beach Vulcan II XP Review: Clicky Compromise
articles.content: Great for typing and fine for gaming, but too many compromises keep this mechanical keyboard from leveling up your play.
articles.summary: WIRED评测Turtle Beach Vulcan II XP机械键盘：打字体验佳、游戏表现尚可，但妥协过多难称升级。

articles.title: TDM Neo Hybrid Headphones Review: Two-in-One Woes
articles.content: CES 2026 loved these innovative headphones that transform into a Bluetooth speaker. After living with them, I’m impressed by the engineering, but less impressed by the sound.

articles.summary: 基督教约会应用Upward重新上线，推出“骑士精神模式”和“婚姻时间表”，向Z世代推销传统价值观。

articles.title: What Type of Mattress Is Right for You? (2026)
articles.content: Here’s how to pick the best mattress for your sleep needs, straight from a professional mattress tester.
articles.summary: WIRED由专业床垫测试师分享选购指南，帮助读者按睡眠需求挑选合适床垫。

articles.title: CSIRO Uses Serverless Architecture to Query 100x More Genomic Variants on AWS
articles.content: CSIRO has developed Serverless Beacon, a serverless architecture for querying genomic variants without copying VCF files into a central database. The system combines Amazon S3, Lambda, Athena and DynamoDB, using metadata indexes and HTTP byte range requests to query compressed genomic regions. Tests reported 1.52 second average latency for 10,000 base pair queries. By Leela Kumili
articles.summary: CSIRO基于AWS构建无服务器架构Serverless Beacon，无需集中入库即可查询基因组变异，查询量提升百倍。

articles.title: AWS Introduces Lambda Web Functions for Node.js Applications
articles.content: AWS recently introduced Lambda Web Functions, allowing developers to run Node.js web applications using frameworks such as Express and Hono directly on Lambda, with support for concurrent requests and response streaming. By Renato Losio
articles.summary: AWS推出Lambda Web Functions，支持Express、Hono等Node.js框架直接在Lambda运行，并支持并发请求与流式响应。

articles.title: Cloudflare Brings On-Demand CPU and Memory Profiling to Production Workers
articles.content: Cloudflare has introduced on-demand CPU and memory profiling for Workers and Durable Objects, allowing developers to investigate performance bottlenecks in production using interactive flamegraphs. By Craig Risi
articles.summary: Cloudflare为Workers和Durable Objects推出按需CPU与内存性能分析，开发者可用交互式火焰图排查生产瓶颈。

articles.title: Article: Multi-Cloud FinOps: An Engineering Framework for Cross-Cloud Cost Optimization
articles.content: Multi-cloud flexibility comes with hidden egress costs driven by service placement and communication patterns. This article applies Backend FinOps to cross-cloud architecture, covering cost visibility through FOCUS, workload placement, synchronization models, and CI/CD-integrated cost governance. A controlled experiment shows architecture changes saved far more than rate negotiation alone. By Vivek Arora
articles.summary: InfoQ文章提出多云FinOps工程框架，通过FOCUS成本可视化、工作负载布局与CI/CD成本治理优化跨云开支。

articles.title: Presentation: Move Fast, Don’t Break Trust: Shipping Constantly with Humans and Beyond
articles.content: Suhail Patel discusses how Monzo structures its software engineering organization and technical stack to ship safely hundreds of times a day. He shares insights into opinionated microservice abstractions, tenancy-based staging, static analysis checks, continuous profiling, demonstrating how a strong internal platform enables engineers and LLMs to iterate rapidly without sacrificing reliability. By Suhail Patel
articles.summary: Monzo工程师Suhail Patel分享如何通过微服务抽象、多租户预发环境和持续性能分析实现每日数百次安全发布。

articles.title: Anthropic Adds Opt-In Security Scanning for Critical Open-Source Projects
articles.content: AI company Anthropic has launched OSS Scanner, a free, opt-in service to find vulnerabilities in open-source projects. Enrolled maintainers receive periodic security reports generated by the company's strongest models, including Claude Mythos. The reports are sent without human review, and project maintainers can choose to validate their findings and decide which proposed fixes to accept. By Matt Saunders
articles.summary: Anthropic推出免费可选OSS Scanner，用其最强模型为关键开源项目定期生成漏洞报告，报告未经人工审核。

articles.title: NgRx 22: Resource Extensions and Dynamic Deep Signals for Angular
articles.content: NgRx 22 adds experimental resource extensions that change Angular's resource behavior, so value() is retained during reloads and no longer throws on errors. It also introduces dynamic deep signals for union types, a SignalStoreFeatureType utility, and ESLint v10 support. Upgrading requires Angular 22 and TypeScript 6.0, and most breaking changes have automated migrations. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: NgRx 22 为 Angular 引入实验性资源扩展，重载时保留值且错误不再抛出，并新增动态深度信号与 ESLint v10 支持。

articles.title: Study Finds AI-generated Code Fails to Boost Productivity Due to Downstream Bottlenecks
articles.content: A recent Harvard study of 718 firms, using the Jellyfish analytics platform, finds that although AI coding assistants and agents increase code volume, this does not translate into a corresponding increase in completed work, partly because AI-generated code increases the workload in later stages of development, particularly code review. By Sergio De Simone
articles.summary: 哈佛研究 718 家企业发现，AI 编程助手虽提升代码量，却因下游环节瓶颈未能带来相应产出增长。

articles.title: Presentation: Actors for Agents: Patterns for Production AI
articles.content: Manju Rajashekhar explains how the actor model solves the complex runtime challenges of production AI agents. By treating agents as distributed systems, he discusses state ownership, message passing, write-through state, and supervision boundaries to manage failures, continuations, and mutable execution graphs, moving agentic workflows beyond fragile demos to resilient architecture. By Manju Rajashekhar
articles.summary: Manju Rajashekhar 分享用 Actor 模型解决生产级 AI 智能体运行时难题，涵盖状态归属、消息传递与故障监管。

articles.title: Vercel Labs Open-Sources fx: a Zig Coding Agent Designed to Be Embedded
articles.content: Vercel Labs has released fx, an experimental open-source coding agent written in Zig. It runs as a CLI, a script component, or an embedded library, including a WebAssembly build. Early feedback questioned its model-agnostic claim and a name conflict with an existing tool. Vercel says the project is pre-1.0 and changing quickly. By Daniel Curtis
articles.summary: Vercel Labs 开源 Zig 编写的编码智能体 fx，可作为 CLI、脚本组件或嵌入式库运行，含 WebAssembly 构建。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #540: AI is finding software flaws faster than teams can fix them
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past two weeks, drawn from our Use-Case Library and from SEC filings. Three things stand out: AI now finds security flaws at record volume, AI agents do a large share of the work at some companies, and test agents keep doing things nobody asked them to do.
articles.summary: AI Weekly 指出 AI 发现安全漏洞的速度已超过团队修复能力，智能体承担大量工作，测试智能体持续增长。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #539: AI-made midterm ads top $137 million, and 70% carry no AI label
articles.content: Campaigns and PACs have spent more than $137 million on AI-generated or AI-enhanced midterm ads, and about 70% of them carry no AI label, the New York Times reported. The biggest pro-AI super PAC network paid about $20 million to a Nevada company that exists only as a post office box. A new report found 81 of 134 AI models failed a test built from terrorist-style questions. A video game reverse engineering site is closing because AI made the work too easy. Some companies that rushed into AI are now limiting it, and a JAMA study counted 270 million questions doctors asked one AI tool. In the middle: police in Michigan used an AI-generated photo of a teenager to catch a suspect.
articles.summary: 中期选举中 AI 生成或增强广告支出超 1.37 亿美元，约 70% 未标注 AI 来源。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #537: AI models may soon copy themselves onto smart fridges, Anthropic says
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared most since our last issue on October 8, minus the stories we already sent you in the Daily Espresso. The most shared: Anthropic's warning that small AI models may soon be able to copy themselves onto home devices. Also: a large study of what AI coding agents change at real companies, a fight over how to check AI math proofs, creative workers pushing back on AI, and police buying more AI.
articles.summary: Anthropic 警告小型 AI 模型可能很快能自我复制到智能冰箱等家用设备上。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #536: Top AI models failed a test of inventing new AI research
articles.content: This issue is built from the links the AI experts we follow shared over the past three days. Most of them look ahead: whether AI can do AI research on its own, who gets a say in governing it, how it is moving into war planning, and how it is moving onto personal computers.
articles.summary: 顶级 AI 模型在自主开展 AI 研究的测试中失败，引发对 AI 治理与军事应用的讨论。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #535: AI got too expensive, so companies are moving to cheaper models
articles.content: This Applied AI edition looks at what organizations actually did with AI over the past three weeks. Three patterns stand out: companies switching models to control cost, large deployments that are now in daily use, and a growing list of places where AI was restricted or removed.
articles.summary: 因 AI 成本过高，企业开始转向更便宜的模型，同时大型部署进入日常使用，部分场景开始限制 AI。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #534: Universities cannot grade their way out of AI
articles.content: This week, campus IT leaders voted AI their top priority for the first time, Cambridge refused Turnitin's new terms over AI training on student work, Dartmouth opened an investigation into its own provost's writing, and Ken Griffin gave Carnegie Mellon $3 billion. Student AI use is no longer a future scenario. The useful question for universities is whether they can teach students to work with AI and still certify what those students can do without it. New evidence from tutoring trials, assessment redesigns, student-support systems and campus data deals points to a practical answer.
articles.summary: 高校 IT 负责人首次将 AI 列为首要任务，剑桥拒绝 Turnitin 新条款，学生 AI 使用已成常态。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #533: Meta tested human callers behind its AI phone agent
articles.content: The AI story of September 22–28 was not simply that agents became more capable. It was that their hidden handoffs became visible: a supposedly automated call could reach a contractor, a supposedly private prompt or image could reach a reviewer, a monitor could detect an agent long before a person stopped it, and a local app flaw could inherit every permission a user had granted. The new AI Weekly Who’s Who census points to one practical question: when an agent crosses a boundary, who knows—and who can still intervene?
articles.summary: Meta 被曝其 AI 电话智能体背后有人工接线员，揭示自动化系统隐藏的人工转接环节。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #531: AI labs shipped agents before agreeing how to report failures
articles.content: The AI story of September 14–20 was not one spectacular model launch. It was the machinery around agents becoming visible: people reading private chats, models writing instructions into their own memory, plugins updating beneath users, and regulators asking how to stop a system after release. The latest AI Weekly Who’s Who census surfaced 535 expert-shared links. We ranked them by consequence and reader relevance, not by raw share count. Here is what mattered last week—and, more importantly, what could move the story from September 22–28.
articles.summary: AI 实验室在未就故障报告方式达成一致前便发布智能体，人工审阅私聊、插件静默更新等问题浮现。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #530: Applied AI This Week
articles.content: Companies are giving AI specific jobs: checking security cameras, helping farmers understand their records, searching satellite images, and preparing sales quotes. This edition explains how those tools work, who can use them, and what companies have reported so far.
articles.summary: 企业为 AI 分配具体任务，如监控摄像头、辅助农户、搜索卫星图像和准备销售报价。

articles.title: AI Weekly Issue #529: OpenAI faces 50-plus lawsuits over alleged ChatGPT harm
articles.content: Thirty new complaints come from survivors of a Canadian school shooting. They accuse OpenAI of failing to warn police; the company disputes key claims.
articles.summary: OpenAI 因 ChatGPT 涉嫌造成伤害面临 50 多起诉讼，其中 30 起来自加拿大校园枪击案幸存者。

articles.title: Building what's next
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Zeno Rocha, CEO of Resend, about scaling "boring" email to 3 million users, the secret Go rewrite behind it, and building for agents. We cover pricing.md, MCP, spam gangs, and why Resend keeps what's next for email.
articles.summary: Resend CEO Zeno Rocha 分享如何将邮件服务扩展至 300 万用户，包括 Go 重写、面向智能体构建及定价策略。

articles.title: From zero to NanoClaw
articles.content: Gavriel Cohen, creator of NanoClaw and co-founder of NanoCo, joins Adam to explain how a 40-hour weekend project became a viral open source hit and the foundation of an enterprise AI company. Gavriel describes the security concerns that led him to build a small, container-isolated alternative to OpenClaw, why he released it under the MIT license, and why the project's community and credibility are more valuable than keeping its code private. They explore the shift from writing code to architecting the environments in which agents work, NanoClaw's "skills over features" approach, the approval and governance layers required inside large companies, and a future where every worker manages agents without surrendering human judgment. They close with the technical simplicity behind NanoClaw, containers, TypeScript, SQLite, and a two-database design, and Adam's case for durable Agent Flow artifacts that keep organizational context from disappearing into chat.
articles.summary: NanoClaw 作者讲述一个周末项目如何成为爆火开源项目，并发展为专注安全隔离的企业 AI 公司。

articles.title: Changelog IRL @ PlanetScale (Sept 17, 2026)
articles.content: Changelog is taking over PlanetScale's HQ We’re getting together IRL!! On Thursday, September 17th, Changelog is taking over PlanetScale’s HQ in San Francisco for an evening of short talks and conversations about AI, developer tools and what people are building. We’ll have a few conversations with special guests and time for questions, food, drinks and hanging out. PlanetScale HQ, 108 Natoma St, San Francisco.
articles.summary: Changelog 将在 PlanetScale 旧金山总部举办线下活动，围绕 AI、开发工具与开发者构建展开分享交流。

articles.title: Forking Cal.com to closed source
articles.content: This week I'm joined by Peer Richelsen, co-founder of Cal.com. What if the majority of open source repositories are already compromised and we just don't know it yet? That's the theory Peer brings to the table this week. We dig into how AI has flattened the knowledge graph to the point that a 16-year-old can vibe hack a power station just as easily as their mom can vibe code an iOS app, why the reporting culture that has kept open source safe all these years is collapsing under AI generated noise, Cal.com's move to fork its own codebase and take the sensitive parts private, and the eye opening reality that shipping "$1 of AI tokens for pennies on the dollar" is now a common startup business model.
articles.summary: Cal.com 联合创始人 Peer Richelsen 讨论开源仓库可能已被普遍攻陷的猜想，以及 AI 对知识图谱的影响。

articles.title: Postgres at PlanetScale
articles.content: Sam Lambert is back after 4 years and he does not hold back! We cover $5 PlanetScale Postgres, the Neki "do-over" of Vitess, agents shipping schema changes through deploy requests, rolling back a 500TB table in seconds, and the very real question of whether to open source any of it. Plus: why he thinks the sleeping, lazy giants should be broken up.
articles.summary: PlanetScale 的 Sam Lambert 介绍 5 美元 Postgres 服务、Vitess 重做及智能体提交 schema 变更等新进展。

articles.title: Canary tokens and digital tripwires
articles.content: Haroon Meer is back! Haroon is the Founder of Thinkst, the ~50-person bootstrapped company behind Canary and Canarytokens — honeypots and tripwires you sprinkle inside your network and forget about until an attacker touches one. We talk about the AWS API key token attackers just can't resist trying, the real credit card token backed by an actual bank partnership, Breadcrumbs (their brand-new feature that leads intruders straight to your canaries), a live demo where a hardware Canary becomes a Synology NAS in one click, and how a company with zero outbound sales and no price increase in ten years quietly passed $22.5 million in ARR.
articles.summary: Thinkst 创始人 Haroon Meer 介绍 Canary 蜜罐与诱饵令牌，讲述如何用数字绊线发现入侵者。

articles.title: From open source hits to OpenAI
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Max Stoiber, currently working on ChatGPT's plugin directory and app platform at OpenAI. We discuss the hundreds of open source projects nobody remembers alongside the big ones like react-boilerplate and styled-components, how Spectrum became part of GitHub and eventually helped shape GitHub Discussions, the founder growth that came from building Stellate, the GraphQL cache that turned into a dual acquisition by Shopify and The Guild, and why ChatGPT apps feel like a new surface for software.
articles.summary: 现于 OpenAI 负责 ChatGPT 插件平台的 Max Stoiber 回顾其开源项目经历，以及从 Spectrum 到 GitHub 的历程。

articles.title: MCP on Code Mode
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Matt Carey about Code Mode and how most of us have been thinking about MCP all wrong. Matt works on the Agents SDK and MCP at Cloudflare — we discuss how server-side Code Mode lets one MCP server expose all ~2,500 Cloudflare API endpoints in about 1,000 tokens of context, the dynamic Worker loader that runs model-written code safely in a V8 isolate, Matt's own workflow with Claude, where memory fits into the future of agents, and his Zaggy git wrapper that keeps agents from force-pushing his repos.

articles.title: Automation at the speed of Swamp
articles.content: This week I'm talking with Adam Jacob, founder of System Initiative and creator of Swamp, about what happens when AI agents change the entire shape of software development. We discuss how he went from an 18-person team down to five and shipped Swamp 900 times in four weeks, why he brought User Acceptance Testing (UAT) testing back from the 90s, why software architecture (and domain-driven design) suddenly matters more than knowing how to write code, the live demo where I pointed Swamp at my Proxmox box and watched it write its own automation (blew my mind!!), and why he'll never accept a pull request to Swamp, ever.

articles.title: Singapore Boffins Weave a GUI Into Fabric
articles.content: Researchers at the National University of Singapore have developed a machine-washable electronic fabric that can turn clothing into an interactive graphical user interface. The prototype reportedly survived 50 gentle machine washes and 1,000 bending cycles, though it still relies on external batteries and controllers. The Register reports: The development could lead - at some point - to a "future in which clothing functions as a pervasive, multimodal human-computer interface," according to the study published in peer-reviewed science journal Nature this week. The paper shows someone interacting with computing devices using the sleeve of a wool sweater (no jokes about the Windows ugly sweater please, this is serious). The researchers, led by Singapore National University research engineer Fu Heng, claim this is a big leap forward. "This fiber-centric approach shifts wearable electronics from flexible panels toward truly textile-native architectures, laying the groundwork for fabrics that visualize, sense, communicate and compute as naturally as the garments they inhabit," the paper says. The researchers claim to have developed a scalable process to make millimeter-thick fibers. Using lasers to strip the insulation from specific spots on the thin copper wires, they attached light-emitting chips to the exposed sections, creating electrical connections to the chips. Thousands of chips were connected to the wires with extreme precision using this process. The fibers were then fed into a transparent plastic tube, and made pressure-sensitive by adding two strips of a compressible, conductive polymer into a second longitudinal channel in the tube. The paper says they could make fibers 10 meters long using this method, and that they are thin and flexible enough to be woven into or attached to fabrics. The researchers were also able to add "peripherals" such as a microphone, a speaker, a temperature sensor and a light sensor. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 新加坡国立大学团队研发出可机洗电子织物，能将衣物变成交互式图形界面，已通过 50 次洗涤测试。

articles.title: People Are Vibe Coding Their Way to Better TVs
articles.content: Frustrated by intrusive ads, sluggish interfaces, and data tracking, smart TV owners are using AI coding tools and open-source projects to strip unwanted software from their televisions and build customized home screens. The Verge reports: Several vibe-coded TV-debloating projects exploded in popularity over the weekend. Cleanyourtv (known as tv-vibehack until the 19th), tv-detox, and dumbtv all claim to accomplish similar things -- remove sponsored ads, debloat the TV so it runs faster, and block unwanted data collection that tracks what you're watching -- without hacking, or rooting, the TV. By default, they all also replace the TV's built-in app launcher with simpler ones. Many users are going a step further and vibe-coding their own replacement launchers, like the Pokemon one below. Most of the projects we've seen so far focus on TVs that run on Android and Google TV operating systems (such as TCL, Hisense, Sony, and older Amazon Fire products), using existing developer modes and the Android Debug Bridge (ADB) to tweak settings and apply (and remove) packages. According to the GitHub pages, they can also work with some Fire TV products that use a custom fork of Android (although likely not on the new Vega-based Fire TV Sticks). Because they use built-in developer tools, they don't require root access or firmware hacking, and they're reversible. Even projects that totally change the look of the interface just use Android's ability to install custom launchers -- in many cases with an assist from Claude Code or a similar tool to create the new launcher, too. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 智能电视用户用 AI 编程工具和开源项目去除广告与追踪软件，自建主屏幕，多个项目迅速走红。

articles.title: Greece Enacts Social Media Ban For Kids Under 15
articles.content: Greece has passed a law banning children under 15 from social media platforms beginning January 1, 2027. The legislation requires platforms to implement reliable age verification and parents to use government-backed apps to restrict access, with penalties for noncompliance under the EU's Digital Services Act. Engadget reports: "It would have been very easy to do absolutely nothing today and wait for the perfect European law. But the challenge is here. Children are sinking into the internet every day, and I believe a responsible government must do what it is obliged to do," said Greece's digital governance and AI minister, Dimitris Papastergiou. The legislation was opposed by Greece's minority parties, so Mitsotakis used his majority government to pass the bill. The nation previously barred mobile phones in schools in 2024, and opinion polls show that the new social media ban for children is widely supported by Greece's adult population. Mitsotakis previously said that his government's "goal is to push the European Union in this direction as well." Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 希腊通过法律，自 2027 年起禁止 15 岁以下儿童使用社交媒体，要求平台进行年龄验证并设处罚。

articles.title: SpaceX In Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites For New Network
articles.content: SpaceX is reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 cellular tower sites across the U.S. as it prepares to launch Starlink Mobile as a fourth nationwide wireless carrier. "We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there's broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call this week. Satellite launches plus spectrum acquisition "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," he said. Bloomberg reports: One of the companies they're in talks with is Crown Castle, which, along with American Tower and Vertical Bridge Holdings, are among the largest owners of cellular towers. When asked on a Wednesday earnings conference call whether Crown Castle is discussing leases with SpaceX, Amazon.com or other satellite-based telecom providers, Chief Executive Officer Chris Hillabrant said, "You can assume that we're talking to all parties." He declined to discuss specific customer details. Mobile networks rely on antennas placed on towers across the country to transmit wireless signals. Carriers such as AT&T Inc., Verizon Communications Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. typically lease room for their equipment at the tower sites because it's more cost effective than owning and maintaining them, in part because the facilities can be shared. The value of the deals with SpaceX could reach into the billions. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: SpaceX 正洽谈接入美国至少 8 万个基站站点，为推出 Starlink Mobile 第四大全国无线运营商铺路。

articles.title: Left Alone With Nothing To Do, AI Agents Started Playing
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: AI agents left to explore a virtual island without a specific task began inventing challenges of their own. MIT researchers say the behavior bears the hallmarks of play. The researchers put 13 AI agents called Eko, each running on Claude Opus 4.7, alone on a simulated desert island for 30 hours. They describe the experiment in a paper posted on arXiv, a site where researchers share studies before peer review. Afterward, they gave the agents specific challenges, like getting as many objects as possible onto the island's tallest rock spire. The Eko agents that had spent those 30 hours playing generally beat identical agents that had never set foot on the island. Today, developers decide in advance what AI should practice and what counts as success. The researchers see this technique -- exploring without a goal -- as a different way for AI agents to learn skills, especially skills that could one day be used to control robots. "We normally develop artificial agents by deciding in advance what they should practice, what they should optimize, and what counts as progress," the researchers write in their report. "Play suggests another regime: give an agent a sufficiently rich and safe world, let it choose what is interesting, and allow useful knowledge to accumulate from the history that follows." UC Berkeley cognitive scientist Eunice Yiu told MIT Technology Review she was impressed with the findings but that more evidence is needed to determine whether AI models are genuinely playing. "It could be the case that the models are genuinely playing, but we don't know based on the paper," says Yiu. "If you only have the behavioral piece, it could be the case that they're just trying to abide by the prompt, trying to imitate humans." MIT professor and coauthor of the paper, Phillip Isola, added: "It's not like this is a system that just suddenly magically decided to play. It's an artifact that learned from our culture, was tra
articles.summary: MIT 研究发现，13 个 AI 智能体在无任务的虚拟岛屿上自发创造挑战并玩耍，表现出类似游戏的行为特征。

articles.title: Microsoft Announces Per-Hour Cost for Xbox Cloud Gaming Service
articles.content: Microsoft has revealed pay-as-you-go pricing for Xbox Cloud Gaming, with introductory packages costing $3.99 for 10 hours, $7.99 for 25 hours, or $11.99 for 50 hours. Starting in November, Game Pass subscribers will receive only 5 to 15 included cloud-gaming hours depending on their tier and will have to buy additional time -- even to stream games they've already purchased. Gizmodo reports: Back in September, before these changes were announced, you paid full purchase price for a game that isn't in the Game Pass library on the assumption that you'd be able to play it via cloud streaming. Maybe your hardware doesn't meet the specs for this fancy new game. Maybe your gaming PC exploded/got stuck on a ship/had a component fail. Maybe you just want to be able to play it in bed on your laptop. Whatever. Now you find that in addition to the cost of the game you bought, you're going to be paying by the hour to play it once your monthly allotment of hours is up. If this is you, I expect you're not particularly amused. Thankfully, Microsoft notes that the playtime you purchase "remains available until it's used," so you won't have to worry about losing any unused time between gaming sessions. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
articles.summary: 微软公布 Xbox 云游戏按小时计费方案，10/25/50 小时套餐分别 3.99/7.99/11.99 美元，11 月起 Game Pass 订阅者仅含 5-15 小时。

articles.title: Ukraine Is Wiping Out Data Centers Across the Border
articles.content: Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged three major Yandex data centers as well as facilities serving Sberbank and VKontakte (the country's equivalent to Facebook), disrupting cloud services, banking, e-commerce, ride-hailing and other digital services across Russia. The attacks may deal a longer-lasting blow to Russia's AI ambitions: Yandex's affected facilities housed its three top-500 supercomputers, and experts say sanctions and shortages of high-end Nvidia chips could make repairs difficult or even take years. "This effectively sets Russia far behind in the AI race, "said Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society activist group. Fortune reports: Data centers are the latest targets of aerial campaigns waged by both sides against each other's vital infrastructure. [...] Kyiv's attacks on Russian data centers closely followed Moscow's recent strikes on data centers in Ukraine, which disrupted the internet and TV broadcasts. On Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones hit a Yandex data center in Sasovo in the Ryazan region that houses two of the company's three supercomputers. A data center in Kaluga was hit a day later and the one in Vladimir was struck Oct. 11. The data center and AI hub for Sberbank was hit Oct. 14 in Balakovo in the Saratov region, and four days later, Kyiv struck a data center in St. Petersburg serving VKontakte. While oil refineries and warehouses are easy prey, data centers are even softer targets -- massive buildings packed with servers and supporting power and cooling infrastructure. Lasting damage can result from a drone carrying a relatively light load of explosives. [...] Ukraine has stored critical data on servers in allied European countries, helping limit the damage from Russian attacks. But Moscow's strict digital sovereignty policy requires all data storage at home, making it extremely vulnerable. "Because all the infrastructure and all the data is located inside Russia, it's relatively easier to take down," [said Nick Reiners, senior
articles.summary: 乌克兰无人机袭击损毁 Yandex 三座数据中心及 Sberbank、VKontakte 设施，导致俄罗斯云服务、银行、电商和出行等数字服务中断。

articles.title: Comcast Loses More Customers, Claims Other ISPs' Cheap Prices Are 'Irrational'
articles.content: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today. Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory. "Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity," Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call. Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said "irrational pricing" from fiber operators includes $30 to $40 monthly broadband offers "in specific markets in the third quarter." He said $30 to $40 pricing is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, and is "getting more expensive with construction costs up as you get into more suburban and rural areas." "As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition," Armstrong said. While he didn't name any specific competitors, Verizon has been pitching FiOS fiber plans that start at $30 a month. Comcast's network is a mix of fiber and cable, and it offers fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory. Armstrong said more Comcast customers are leaving when they face "pricing transitions," apparently referring to the price hikes customers get when promotional offers expire. "We've been refining our offers and retention strategies to better manage these transitions and strengthen customer retention," he said. Cavanagh said that "satellite is not yet a material factor" in the competition Comcast faces, but that Comcast is focused on "anticipating emerging forms of competitio
articles.summary: Comcast 第三季度流失 14.4 万宽带用户，计划裁减有线部门岗位，并称其他 ISP 的低价策略“不理性”。

articles.title: Physicists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle For a Month
articles.content: Physicists at Northwestern University have successfully trapped a single positron for an entire month, allowing researchers to study its quantum properties with unprecedented precision. "Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter, when things could have presumably gone either way," reports Scientific American. From the report: Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron -- the antimatter counterpart of the electron. "The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them," says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters (PDF). The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. "Every time they bang into something, there's a chance of annihilation, but it doesn't always happen," Gabrielse says. "If they make it to the end, they get popped out." Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. "If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls," Gabrielse says. This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a monthâ"and could let them do so indefinitely. The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron's magnetic moment -- basically the strength an
articles.summary: 西北大学物理学家将单个正电子成功囚禁一个月，可高精度研究其量子特性，或有助于揭示物质与反物质不对称之谜。
